title: Who Jesus Is and What It Costs
overview: Jesus feeds another crowd, is challenged by critics and misunderstood by friends, and after Peter names him as the Messiah, he explains that his path leads through suffering and invites his followers to share it.

parts.label: Feeding four thousand (vv. 1-10)
parts.note: After three days with a hungry crowd, Jesus feeds about four thousand people with seven loaves and a few fish, and seven baskets are left over. The previous chapter places him in mostly non-Jewish territory, so many readers think this crowd included outsiders, though the text does not say so directly.

parts.label: A demand for proof (vv. 11-13)
parts.note: The Pharisees, a strict and influential religious group, ask for a sign from heaven, meaning a dramatic proof straight from God, to test him rather than to learn. Jesus sighs deeply and refuses, apparently because they had already seen much and wanted proof on their own terms.

parts.label: Warning about yeast (vv. 14-21)
parts.note: Yeast works quietly through a whole batch of dough, so it was a common picture for an influence that spreads unnoticed, here the outlook of the Pharisees and of Herod, the local ruler. The disciples think he means their forgotten bread, and Jesus reminds them of the leftover baskets to show they still miss what the feedings reveal about him.

parts.label: A blind man healed slowly (vv. 22-26)
parts.note: Unusually, this healing happens in two stages, with blurry sight first and clear sight after a second touch. Many interpreters see it as a picture of the disciples, who are about to see partly who Jesus is but not yet clearly.

parts.label: Peter names the Messiah (vv. 27-33)
parts.note: Peter calls Jesus the Messiah, God's promised king, but when Jesus says he must be rejected, killed and rise again, Peter scolds him. Jesus calls Peter 'Satan', meaning an opponent, because Peter is trying to steer him away from the suffering Jesus says is God's plan.

parts.label: The cost of following (vv. 34-38)
parts.note: Rome executed people by crucifixion and made the condemned carry their own crossbeam, so telling followers to take up their cross meant being ready to give up even their life to follow him. He argues that clinging to life on your own terms ends up losing it, since nothing in the whole world is worth trading your life for.

think: What would you be willing to lose for something you were convinced was true, and where would you draw the line?
